messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 64
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 64, Rajiv had spent most of his working life in warehouses and loading docks, a steady routine that he valued for its predictability. Before the assault that changed him, he had been the kind of man who rose early, took pride in getting to work on time, and came home tired but settled. The trauma happened overseas during a period when he had been held captive, and even now he did not describe it in abstract terms so much as in fragments of lived time: the hours stretching on in a place where he could not leave, the feeling that every sound outside the room meant someone was coming in, and the particular dread of the late evening when the day had the same shape it had on the worst day of his life. When he was retelling it, he would fixate on how close he had felt to snakes as well, and how any mention of them brought the whole memory sharply into view. He had seen them then, and since returning home even a conversation about snakes, or a photo flashed on a phone, could make his body tighten before he had time to stop it.

In the weeks after he came home, Rajiv found that darkness became difficult to tolerate. Going to bed meant more than rest; it meant lying still and waiting for the dark to close in, and he would postpone sleep as long as he could by sitting up in the living room, turning on the television without really watching it, or remaining on his feet until he felt exhausted enough to collapse into bed. If he woke in the middle of the night, especially in a dark room, he would lie rigid and listen, certain that the hours after dusk were when he was least safe. He kept asking his wife whether he was all right, whether his heart was beating normally, whether she thought he looked pale or unsteady. He also began checking his body over and over for signs of danger or injury, pressing at his arms, chest, and legs as if he needed to confirm that nothing hidden was happening to him. The checking did not reassure him for long, but he returned to it anyway, trying to make sense of the feeling that his body might betray him without warning.

At work, Rajiv remained in the warehouse, but the job no longer felt simple. He became intensely watchful while moving through the loading areas, repeatedly looking behind him, especially if he had to cross a quieter stretch between shelves or step outside near the end of a shift. If someone walked up from behind, he startled more than he used to, and he found himself scanning entrances and exits automatically, as though danger could appear from any angle. The warehouse’s changing light across the day mattered to him in a way it had not before. As evening approached and the sky darkened, he felt the sense of unease build; the same time of day that matched the captivity period now seemed to pull him back toward it. He would notice the clock, notice the thinning light through the dock doors, and feel his attention sharpen uncomfortably, as though he needed to be ready for something he could not name. That watchfulness carried into his commute and into his walks from the parking lot, where he frequently checked over his shoulder for anyone following him.

Over time, Rajiv’s way of coping narrowed his life. He avoided lying in the dark, delayed bedtime, and leaned on his wife and adult children for repeated reassurance, asking the same questions more than once because the comfort never lasted long enough. He also tried hard not to think about what had happened to him. When the memory began to surface, he would push it away quickly, certain that if he let himself dwell on it, he would not be able to handle what came next. Even so, the thoughts returned in flashes, especially at night, and he came to believe with growing hopelessness that he could not stop bad things from happening to him. He said this quietly, without drama, but with a tired finality that made clear how deeply he had come to accept it. More than once, he admitted that he was not sure his life was worth living anymore, not because he wanted to die in a planned way, but because the effort of keeping himself together had begun to feel endless.

By the time he sought help, Rajiv’s symptoms had become difficult to hide from the people around him. His wife had noticed the nightly restlessness, the repeated reassurance-seeking, and the way he sat up or paced instead of going to bed. At work, he was still reliable, but he was slower at settling into tasks and more distracted by scanning the room and checking behind him. What finally brought him in was a combination of exhaustion and fear: he was worried that he could not keep enduring the nights in the dark and afraid that if his mind returned fully to the captivity, he would be overwhelmed by it. He came hoping for relief, but more than that, he hoped someone could help him feel safe enough to sleep again and to believe, even a little, that the future was still his to live.
